subject: Connectivity architecture choices for Private Deployment - VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Simon Chu <simon.chu@healthnostrum.com>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Cc: netops@healthnostrum.com, procurement@healthnostrum.com
Date: 2026-03-15T09:12:00-04:00
Subject: Connectivity options for Private Deployment

Marcus —

Thanks again for the product walkthrough yesterday. To follow up: HealthNostrum is evaluating a private deployment of Redwood in our AWS account (us-east-1). We need a connectivity approach that meets our compliance needs (no public egress for inference traffic), keeps latency under ~20ms for our UI calls, and minimizes operational complexity.

High-level constraints:
- Multi-account setup: our App and Data accounts are separate; we prefer a model that avoids complex cross-account routing where possible.
- Security: we require private endpoints and ability to audit flow logs.
- Availability: we'd like an RTO of <30m for networking issues; optional redundant path is fine.

Can you outline tradeoffs between VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN for our use case? Any preference from Redwood's side given production SLAs?

Simon Chu
Director of Engineering, HealthNostrum
From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: Simon Chu <simon.chu@healthnostrum.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-15T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Connectivity options for Private Deployment

Hi Simon —

Appreciate the constraints summary. Looping in Karthik (infra) and Lauren (acct lead) so we can give a concise recommendation. Quick summary from us:

- VPC Peering: simplest for same-account or tightly controlled cross-account peering, low latency, no intermediate NAT, but not transitive and can get heavy to manage at scale. Good if you run Redwood in the same AWS account or want direct routing between subnets.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): provides per-service private endpoints across accounts/regions with strong isolation and easier IAM access controls. Slightly higher per-GB cost and small additional egress latency, but scales well for multi-account setups and aligns with zero-public-egress policies.
- Site-to-Site VPN: lowest barrier if you need to connect on-prem or an external network; typically higher latency and less reliable than cloud-native options. Useful as a backup path (redundant) but not ideal as primary for low-latency UIs.

Karthik — can you sketch the operational and security implications (logs, KMS, endpoint management) and drop any cost/latency numbers you’d expect?

Next steps: Karthik to provide a short pros/cons + attachments; Lauren and I will propose a final recommendation and MAP.

— Marcus
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Cc: Simon Chu <simon.chu@healthnostrum.com>
Date: 2026-03-16T09:30:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Connectivity options for Private Deployment

Marcus / Lauren / Simon —

I put together a rapid technical comparison and attached two artifacts: connectivity-cost-estimate.xlsx and latency-test-plan.md (both attached). Key points:

1) VPC Peering
- Pros: Lowest latency (typically single-digit ms intra-region), no per-request interface fees, direct routing.
- Cons: Non-transitive (if Redwood components and customer subnets span multiple accounts, you'll need multiple peerings), route table management scales poorly, does not support AWS PrivateLink-like granular service authorizations.
- Security: Flow logs via VPC Flow Logs available; needs cross-account IAM management for peering accept/modify.
- When to pick: single-account deploy or small number of peerings where you control both sides.

2) AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints)
- Pros: Strong isolation; works well cross-account without complex route tables; supports service-level access control; integrates with AWS Private DNS; endpoints appear as ENIs in your subnets. Scales for many customers.
- Cons: Per-GB data processing + hours for endpoints -> higher cost at scale. Slightly higher latency (typically 3–8ms overhead) vs peering.
- Security: Supports security groups on endpoints, logs via VPC Flow Logs + ENI tracing; aligns well with no-public-egress policies.
- When to pick: multi-account customers, SaaS-in-account pattern, customers that need per-customer isolation without lots of peering rules.

3) Site-to-Site VPN / Transit Gateway VPN Attachments
- Pros: Flexible for on-prem and for customers not ready to do cross-account cloud networking. Transit Gateway + VPN can centralize.
- Cons: Higher latency and jitter; VPN tunnels can drop and require monitoring; throughput limits unless you use multiple tunnels or AWS-managed hardware.
- Security: IPsec with shared keys or certificates; can be hardened but is operationally heavier.
- When to pick: short term cutover, on-prem access requirement, or as redundant path.

Operational recommendations for HealthNostrum (given requirements):
- Primary: AWS PrivateLink from HealthNostrum account(s) to a dedicated Redwood service endpoint in the HealthNostrum VPC. This avoids transitive routing issues and gives clear service-level access and logging.
- Secondary / Backup: Site-to-site VPN to a transit VPC or Transit Gateway for redundancy. In case of PrivateLink endpoint maintenance or regional failures, fail traffic to VPN (expect higher latency).
- Avoid relying on many VPC Peerings across accounts; if you insist on peering, limit to same-account deployments.

Monitoring / Security:
- Enable VPC Flow Logs + CloudTrail for endpoint operations.
- Use customer-managed KMS keys for any traffic- or artifact-encryption needs and record key usage in our audit logs.
- SLOs: PrivateLink-based path meets sub-20ms goal in most cases; we'll validate with a short latency test (see latency-test-plan.md).

I've attached a quick cost estimate for comparison. Numbers assume 1TB/month of inference traffic; we can re-run for your expected TTM.

Attachments: connectivity-cost-estimate.xlsx, latency-test-plan.md

— Karthik
Infrastructure Engineer
Redwood Inference
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
To: Simon Chu <simon.chu@healthnostrum.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-17T10:00:00-04:00
Subject: Re: Connectivity options for Private Deployment

Simon —

Thanks for the helpful context and thanks Karthik for the detailed breakdown. Summary recommendation from Redwood:

1) Proceed with AWS PrivateLink as the primary connectivity model. It aligns with your multi-account setup, minimizes cross-account route complexity, and supports your no-public-egress requirement. Based on our internal tests (see attached latency plan) we expect application RTT to stay comfortably under 20ms for the user flows you described.

2) Implement a site-to-site VPN to a Transit Gateway as an active-passive backup. We’ll document failover steps; note that during failover customers should expect increased latency and possibly throttle adjustments.

3) Operational items & next steps (Mutual Action Plan attached):
- Schedule a 60-minute technical onboarding with Karthik + your netops (please propose times next week).
- Share expected monthly traffic numbers so we can refine the cost estimate and confirm PrivateLink pricing.
- Provision a customer-managed KMS key for encrypted artifacts and confirm SOC2 access controls required for audit logs.

If you’re agreeable, we’ll create a short runbook for endpoint provisioning, provide Terraform snippets, and open a support channel for the initial 30-day cutover.

Simon — can you confirm the team’s preferred time window for the onboarding call?

Best,
Lauren Bishop
Enterprise Account Executive
Redwood Inference
